chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, the truck and the daily check

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The forklift job and the OSHA training rule
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain who trains and certifies a forklift operator and when retraining is needed.
This lesson builds toward: Using what OSHA requires of employers, you will write a plan to get trained and evaluated and an honest résumé line, that names the employer's role and claims no certification you do not have.
OSHA calls forklifts "powered industrial trucks". Its rule, 29 CFR 1910.178, says the employer must make sure every operator is competent. That means training (classroom and hands-on practice under a qualified trainer) and an evaluation of you driving in the actual workplace.
The employer then certifies that you were trained and evaluated. The record shows your name, the dates of training and evaluation, and who did them. Your evaluation must be repeated at least once every three years.
You also get refresher training if you are seen driving unsafely, have an accident or near miss, get a poor evaluation, are moved to a different type of truck, or the workplace changes in a way that affects safety.
Federal labor rules do not allow anyone under 18 to operate a forklift on the job. And an online course or wallet card alone does not make you certified: only your employer's training and evaluation do.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the U.S. agency for workplace safety.
- Powered industrial truck: OSHA's name for forklifts and similar machines that lift and move loads.
- Evaluation: a qualified person watching you operate in the workplace to judge if you are safe.
- Refresher training: extra training to fix a problem or prepare you for a new truck or workplace.
- Near miss: an event where nobody got hurt but someone could have.
Official sources:
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (the federal forklift rule)
- OSHA eTool: Operator training
- 29 CFR 570.58: No forklift operation by workers under 18 (U.S. Department of Labor rule, Cornell LII copy)
Try it now: On paper, write three sentences in your own words: who trains and evaluates a forklift operator, how often the evaluation is repeated, and two events that mean you need refresher training.
You can now explain who trains and certifies a forklift operator, how often you are evaluated, and when you need refresher training.

check.q: Who must train and evaluate you before you operate a forklift at work?
check.why: OSHA's rule puts training and evaluation on the employer, in the actual workplace.

check.q: You bump a rack with your forklift. Nobody is hurt. What is true?
options: You must buy a new card online
It is a reason for refresher training
check.why: An accident or near miss is one of OSHA's triggers for refresher training.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Forklift types and parts
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the forklift type and name its main parts.
This lesson builds toward: Given pictures or descriptions of forklifts, you will identify the forklift type and point out the main parts, naming at least 6 parts and what each one does.
OSHA groups forklifts into seven classes. Class I: electric rider trucks. Class II: electric narrow-aisle trucks. Class III: electric hand trucks, including walk-behind pallet jacks. Classes IV and V: engine-powered trucks, with cushion tires for smooth indoor floors (IV) or air-filled tires for outdoors (V). Class VI: tractors that tow. Class VII: rough-terrain forklifts for building sites and farms.
Most counterbalance forklifts have the same main parts. The forks lift the load. The forks hang on the carriage, which moves up and down the mast. The load backrest stops the load from falling back toward you. The overhead guard protects you from falling objects. The counterweight at the back balances the load.
In the seat you have the steering, the direction control (forward and reverse), the lift and tilt levers, the horn, the brakes and the seatbelt. The data plate (also called the capacity plate or nameplate) tells you how much the truck can lift.
Words to know:
- Mast: the upright frame the forks travel up and down on.
- Carriage: the plate on the mast that holds the forks.
- Load backrest: a frame above the forks that stops the load falling back toward the operator.
- Overhead guard: the roof frame that protects the operator from falling objects.
- Counterweight: a heavy weight at the back of the truck that balances the load.
- Data plate: the plate on the truck that shows its model and how much it can lift.
Official sources:
- OSHA eTool: Forklift types (Classes I to VII)
- OSHA eTool: Forklift parts
Try it now: Draw a simple side view of a sit-down forklift (boxes and lines are fine). Label at least six parts: forks, carriage, mast, load backrest, overhead guard, counterweight. Next to each, write one line on what it does.
You can now say which class a forklift is in and name its main parts and what they do.

check.q: Which part stops a load from falling back toward the operator?
check.why: The load backrest sits above the forks and keeps the load from falling toward you.

check.q: A forklift built for uneven ground on a building site is which class?
check.why: Class VII are rough-terrain forklifts for uneven outdoor ground.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The pre-shift inspection
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Complete a pre-shift inspection checklist and decide if the truck is safe to use.
This lesson builds toward: Using an inspection checklist, you will complete a pre-shift inspection and decide whether the truck can be used, checking every item and taking any unsafe truck out of service.
OSHA requires every forklift to be examined before it is used, at least once a day; if trucks run around the clock, after every shift. If anything makes the truck unsafe, it is taken out of service until it is repaired.
Start with the key off. Look at fluid levels and for leaks, cracks and damaged hoses or mast chains (never put your hands inside the mast). Check the tires, the forks, the load backrest, the overhead guard, and that the data plate and warning decals are in place and readable. Check the seatbelt.
Electric trucks: look at cables, connectors and the battery restraint. Propane trucks: check the tank is mounted right, the relief valve points up and there are no leaks.
Then, with the truck running, test the brakes, steering, forward and reverse, lift, lower, tilt, horn, lights and back-up alarm. If something is wrong: do not use the truck, tag or report it, write it on the checklist and tell your supervisor. Only trained, authorized people make repairs.
Step by step:
- Key off: fluids, leaks, hoses and chains (look, don't reach in).
- Tires, forks, load backrest, overhead guard.
- Data plate and warning decals present and readable; seatbelt works.
- Key on: brakes, steering, forward and reverse.
- Lift, lower, tilt, horn, lights, back-up alarm.
- Sign the checklist; report and tag any defect and do not use the truck.
Words to know:
- Pre-shift inspection: the check of a forklift before it is used for the shift.
- Out of service: not to be used until it is repaired, usually marked with a tag.
- Mast chains: the chains that lift the carriage and forks up the mast.
Official sources:
- OSHA eTool: Pre-operation inspection
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (the federal forklift rule)
Try it now: Write your own pre-shift checklist with two columns, "Key off" and "Key on", using the OSHA pre-operation page. Then read this practice case: the horn does not work and one fork has a crack. Write what you do, step by step.
You can now complete a pre-shift inspection checklist and take an unsafe truck out of service.

check.q: How often must a forklift be examined before use?
check.why: OSHA requires an examination before use, at least daily, and after each shift for round-the-clock use.

check.q: During your check, the brakes feel weak. What do you do?
options: Report it, tag it out of service and do not use it
Tell a coworker to use it
check.why: An unsafe truck is taken out of service and reported; only authorized people repair it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Loads, driving and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading the data plate and judging a load
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a load is safe to lift using the data plate and load center.
This lesson builds toward: Given a data plate and a load description, you will decide whether the load is safe to lift and explain why, getting at least 4 of 5 load decisions right.
The data plate shows the most the truck can lift at a certain load center. The load center is the distance from the front face of the forks to the middle (center of gravity) of the load. Many forklifts are rated for a 24-inch load center. If the load's middle is farther out than that, or the truck has an attachment, the safe capacity is lower: check the plate and ask your supervisor.
A forklift balances like a seesaw on its front wheels. The load on the forks is on one side; the truck and counterweight are on the other. Too much weight, a load too far out, or a load raised and tilted forward can tip the truck forward. Turning too fast can tip it sideways.
Lift only stable loads within the capacity. Center the load between the forks and put the forks under it at least two-thirds of the load's length. Lift a little, tilt the mast back slightly so the load rests against the backrest, and keep it low.
Step by step:
- Find the weight of the load (label, paperwork or ask).
- Read the data plate: capacity and load center.
- Is the load's middle within the load center? Is the weight under the capacity?
- Is the load stable, wrapped and not damaged?
- If yes: center it, forks at least two-thirds under, lift a little, tilt back. If no or unsure: stop and ask.
Words to know:
- Capacity: the most weight a forklift can safely lift, shown on the data plate.
- Load center: the distance from the front of the forks to the middle of the load.
- Center of gravity: the point where an object's weight is balanced.
- Tipover: when a forklift falls over forward or onto its side.
Official sources:
- OSHA eTool: Load handling
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (the federal forklift rule)
Try it now: Practice only, made-up numbers. A truck's plate says 4,000 lb at a 24-inch load center. Decide yes or no, with a reason: (1) a 3,200 lb pallet, centered and wrapped; (2) a 4,600 lb crate; (3) a 2,500 lb load that is leaning and torn; (4) a 3,000 lb load whose middle is far out past 24 inches. Write what you would do for each.
You can now read a data plate and decide whether a load is safe to lift, and say why.

check.q: The plate says 5,000 lb at 24 inches. The load is 5,800 lb. What do you do?
options: Add a person on the back as extra weight
Do not lift it; tell your supervisor
Lift it high so it balances
check.why: Never lift more than the rated capacity; extra riders are never allowed.

check.q: How far should the forks go under a load?
options: At least two-thirds of the load's length
Through to the next pallet behind it
check.why: OSHA's guidance is at least two-thirds of the load length, without hitting loads behind it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Driving, docks and parking safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose the safe action when driving, at a dock and when parking.
This lesson builds toward: Given a driving, stacking, dock or parking situation, you will choose the safe action under OSHA rules, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
Travel with the load low and tilted back, never raised or tilted forward. Drive at a speed that lets you stop safely, and slow down on wet floors, at turns and at cross aisles. Sound the horn at cross aisles and blind corners. Look where you are going. If the load blocks your view, drive in reverse. Keep about three truck lengths behind another truck.
People: nobody stands or walks under raised forks, loaded or empty. No riders unless the truck has a safe place for them and they are allowed. Never drive toward someone standing in front of a wall or rack.
Ramps: go slowly. With a load, keep the load uphill: drive forward going up and in reverse going down. Never turn on a ramp. Docks: before driving into a trailer, the trailer's brakes must be set and its rear wheels chocked; check the trailer floor for breaks or weak spots; stay away from the dock edge.
Parking: if you leave the truck (or are 25 feet or more away, or it is out of sight), lower the forks all the way, put the controls in neutral, shut it off and set the brake; block the wheels on a slope. If a sit-down truck starts to tip: do not jump. Stay in the seat with the seatbelt on, hold the wheel, brace your feet and lean away from the fall.
Step by step:
- Load low, tilted back; horn at cross aisles; look where you drive.
- Load blocks your view: drive in reverse.
- Ramps: load uphill, no turning on the ramp.
- Docks: trailer brakes set, wheels chocked, floor checked.
- Parking: forks down, neutral, power off, brake set.
- Tipping: stay in, belt on, hold on, lean away.
Words to know:
- Cross aisle: where two aisles meet, like an intersection.
- Wheel chock: a wedge put against a wheel so a trailer cannot roll.
- Dock edge: the edge of the loading dock where the floor drops off.
- Unattended: left alone: 25 feet or more away from the truck, or out of sight of it.
Official sources:
- OSHA eTool: Traveling and maneuvering
- OSHA eTool: Loading docks
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (the federal forklift rule)
Try it now: Make a pocket card with two lists: "Before I drive into a trailer" and "When I park". Then answer this practice case in writing: you are carrying a tall load that blocks your view and you must go down a ramp. What do you do?
You can now choose the safe action when driving, at a dock, on a ramp, when parking and if a truck starts to tip.

check.q: A coworker wants to stand under your raised forks to fix a label. What do you say?
options: "Only if you wear a hard hat."
"No. Nobody goes under raised forks. I'll lower them first."
check.why: OSHA forbids anyone standing or passing under the raised forks, loaded or empty.

check.q: Your sit-down forklift starts to tip over. What do you do?
options: Stay in the seat, belt on, hold the wheel and lean away
check.why: On a sit-down truck, staying in with the seatbelt on is how you avoid being crushed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting trained and hired as a forklift operator
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a plan to get trained and evaluated, and an honest résumé line.
This lesson builds toward: Using what OSHA requires of employers, you will write a plan to get trained and evaluated and an honest résumé line, that names the employer's role and claims no certification you do not have.
Many warehouse, distribution and retail employers hire people for general warehouse work and then train them on forklifts. Some staffing agencies, workforce centers and community colleges also run forklift training with hands-on practice. Ask whether it includes driving under a trainer and a practical evaluation.
Remember: wherever you train, each new employer must make sure you are trained and evaluated for its trucks and its workplace before you drive alone. Prior training helps, and an employer may not need to repeat topics you already learned and were evaluated on.
On your résumé, be honest. If you finished this course, write that you completed forklift safety knowledge training. If an employer trained and evaluated you, write the truck types and the year. Never write "certified" if you were not.
In an interview, talk about the pre-shift check, the data plate and pedestrian safety. Employers want operators who are careful first and fast second.
Step by step:
- List three local employers or programs that train forklift operators (job sites, workforce center, community college).
- Ask each: does it include supervised driving and an evaluation?
- Write an honest résumé line for what you have done so far.
- Practice a 30-second answer: "How do you keep safe on a forklift?"
Words to know:
- Staffing agency: a company that places workers in jobs with other businesses.
- Workforce center: a public office (often called an American Job Center) that helps people find jobs and training.
Official sources:
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (the federal forklift rule)
- OSHA eTool: Operator training
Try it now: Write your plan: three places that could train you, the question you will ask each, one honest résumé line, and your 30-second answer to "How do you keep safe on a forklift?" Read the answer out loud.
You can now write a plan to get forklift training and evaluation and describe your training honestly on a résumé.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Inspection checklist Missing key-off or key-on checks, or no step for an unsafe truck. Covers every key-off and key-on item for the chosen truck type and says what to do with a defect. Adds the extra checks for electric or propane trucks. Parts named Fewer than six parts named, or wrong uses. At least six parts named with what each does, and the truck's class. Explains how the counterweight and load backrest keep the operator safe. Load decisions A load over capacity or unstable is marked safe. All three load decisions are right, with a reason using the data plate. Notes when to ask a supervisor, such as an unknown weight or an attachment. Driving, dock and parking card Missing the dock check or a parking step. Lists the dock steps (brakes, chocks, floor) and all four parking steps. Adds ramp, pedestrian and tipover rules. Training plan and résumé line Claims to be certified, or says no employer training is needed. Names three places to train, says the employer must evaluate, and gives an honest résumé line. Includes a practiced 30-second safety answer for interviews. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check again.

check.q: You finished this course but no employer has evaluated you. Which résumé line is honest?
check.why: It says exactly what you did, without claiming a certification you do not have.

check.q: What should you ask a forklift training program?
options: Whether it includes supervised driving and a practical evaluation
Whether it gives a fancy card
Whether you can skip the hands-on part
Whether it is the cheapest online
check.why: OSHA training includes hands-on practice and an evaluation, so check the program has them.
